author: Anonymous
addressee: Diognetus, a distinguished pagan interested in Christianity
occasion: Diognetus has eagerly asked to learn about the religion of the Christians: what God they trust, how they worship, why they despise the world and death, reject Greek gods and Jewish practice, and love one another. The author writes to answer these questions and to lead him toward Christian faith.
argument: The author first clears away pagan idolatry, showing that the gods are mere corruptible materials. He then argues that Jewish sacrificial worship misunderstands God, who needs nothing, and that Jewish food laws, Sabbath, circumcision, and calendar observance are foolish. Christians are not distinguished by land, language, or customs, yet they live as resident aliens in every homeland, loving all while being persecuted. Their way of life is not a human invention but was revealed by the Creator himself, who sent his Son not to terrify but to save. God bore with human sin until the time he chose, then gave his own Son as a ransom, so that through one righteous man many lawless people might be justified. The author urges Diognetus to desire this faith, know the Father, imitate God's kindness by bearing others' burdens, and so come to true knowledge and life.

outline.move: The author welcomes Diognetus's eager inquiry into Christianity and asks God for help to speak and be heard well.
He urges Diognetus to clear his mind and shows that pagan gods are corruptible, senseless materials, so Christians rightly refuse to worship them.
He argues that Jewish sacrificial worship is misguided because God, the creator and giver of all, needs nothing.
He dismisses Jewish food rules, Sabbath, circumcision, and calendar observance as ridiculous, and says the mystery of Christian piety cannot be learned from a mere human.
He describes Christians as indistinguishable from others in land, language, and customs, yet living as resident aliens who love all and are persecuted by all.
He develops the analogy that Christians are to the world what the soul is to the body: invisible, life-giving, hated, yet holding the world together.
He insists Christianity is no human invention: the invisible Creator himself sent his Son, not with tyranny and fear but in gentleness, to save and persuade.
He argues that no human being knew God before he revealed himself, and that God revealed himself through faith by his beloved Son.
He explains that God bore with human sin until the appointed time, then gave his own Son as a ransom, so that one righteous man might justify many lawless people.
He urges Diognetus to desire this faith, know the Father, and imitate God's kindness by bearing others' burdens and despising the world's deception.
He presents himself as a disciple of the apostles and teacher of the nations, speaking the things revealed by the Word to the faithful.
He closes by urging attentive reading, and uses the trees of knowledge and life in paradise to show that true knowledge and true life belong together.

cast.name: Diognetus
cast.who: The distinguished addressee, a pagan eager to learn about Christianity.

cast.name: The author
cast.who: An anonymous Christian teacher writing as a disciple of the apostles.

cast.name: God the Father
cast.who: The invisible Creator and Lord of all, who sent his Son.

cast.name: The Son
cast.who: God's beloved Son, the Word, sent to reveal God and save humanity.

cast.name: The Word
cast.who: The divine Word, identified with the Son, through whom God reveals himself.

cast.name: The serpent
cast.who: The deceiver in paradise who led the first humans astray.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, mentioned in the closing paradise imagery.

voices.speaker: The apostle (paraphrased)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as 'the apostle' and paraphrased: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.' The text offers a close paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 8:1, not a verbatim quotation, and does not name Paul.

key_terms.sense: Reverent worship or piety toward God, the central subject of Diognetus's inquiry.
Superstitious or fearful religious observance, used negatively of Jewish practice.
The followers of Christ, the new people whose way of life the letter describes.
Way of life or citizenship, especially the Christians' heavenly citizenship lived on earth.
Resident aliens or sojourners, describing Christians' relation to their earthly homelands.
The soul, used as the governing analogy for Christians' place in the world.
The world, both as the created order Christians inhabit and as the hostile order that hates them.
The coming or presence of the Son, especially his future coming as judge.
Ransom, the price paid by God in giving his Son for sinners.
Righteousness, especially the righteousness of the one Son by which many lawless people are justified.
God's kindness or goodness, shown in bearing with sin and saving humanity.
Knowledge, especially true knowledge of God that must be joined with true life.
Life, especially true life in God, contrasted with death and linked to knowledge.
The Word, the divine Son through whom God reveals himself and speaks to the faithful.
The church, the community enriched and taught by the Word.

scripture: The author paraphrases 1 Corinthians 8:1 ('Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up') without naming Paul or quoting verbatim, and alludes to Genesis 2-3 (the trees of knowledge and life in paradise). He refers to 'the Lord's Passover' and to 'the law,' 'the prophets,' 'the gospels,' and 'the apostles' tradition' as recognized categories. No LXX book names or Psalm numbering are explicitly cited.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; the 2nd century is widely accepted but not certain.
The identity of the author; the attribution to an anonymous disciple of the apostles is inferred from the text.
The identity of Diognetus; he may be a historical figure or a literary addressee.
The integrity of the text; sections 7 and 10 contain apparent gaps or corruptions in the manuscript tradition.
Whether the work originally ended at section 10, with sections 11-12 being a later addition or a separate fragment.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The apostle (paraphrased), introduced as 'the apostle' and paraphrased: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ. (section 12)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Remove the attribution to 'the apostle' and note that the passage is a quotation without a speaker label.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: The Greek text contains "υἱός" (e.g., section 7: "υἱὸν"), but the word "παῖς" does not appear in any section.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Delete "παῖς" from the list of source_forms for the Son.
